messages.content:
Story Time for Caregivers 

Emily Davis 

State University 

December 19, 2025 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Abstract 

Early literacy development begins in infancy, yet many caregivers lack awareness of age-appropriate literacy practices beyond shared reading, particularly for children under one year of age. Libraries and pediatric providers are great resources to support early literacy, but existing programs often face barriers to caregiver participation and are typically evaluated only through caregiver surveys instead of evaluating the child’s early literacy skills. This study proposes an evaluation of a library-based early literacy program targeted at caregivers of infants that integrates community partnerships with hospitals, pediatricians, and daycare providers to improve outreach and engagement. The program provides caregivers with books and instructional materials focused on the core early literacy practices of singing, talking, reading, writing, and playing. Two research questions guide the study. The first is whether community partnerships increase caregiver participation in early literacy programs, and the second is whether increased caregiver knowledge of early literacy practices positively affects children’s early literacy skills over time. Caregiver participation will be measured through attendance data. Long-term child outcomes will be evaluated by comparing participants’ kindergarten reading readiness screener results to those of the general population. Statistical analyses will include descriptive statistics and inferential testing using z-scores and two-tailed t-tests. By examining both outreach effectiveness and long-term child literacy outcomes, this study aims to address significant gaps in early literacy research and create evidence based library programming for infants and their caregivers. 

 

 

Introduction 

The first years of a child's life are crucial for developing the foundation of early literacy. However, many who interact with children before they are school aged may not be aware of what early literacy activities look like, especially for children under the age of one. “The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends that pediatric providers promote early literacy development for children beginning in infancy... advising all parents that reading aloud with young children can enhance parent-child relationships and prepare young minds to learn language and early literacy skills” (High, pg 1). Caregivers may be made aware of the importance of early literacy at well-child checkups, but they may not be made aware of what they can do besides reading to their child or what an appropriate choice of book might be. 

While pediatricians may be a resource to encourage early literacy, many libraries offer early literacy programs. These programs can vary from a library tech or librarian reading and singing songs to a group of babies and their caregivers, to full blown educational programs for caregivers. However, many barriers exist for libraries to attract caregivers to these programs. Many programs are done during weekdays during the day when caregivers may be working. Afternoon sessions can be difficult for caregivers as well, since many children under one go to bed early. Another barrier can be caregiver perception of the library and early literacy. Caregivers many not understand the importance of early literacy activities, or how to do early literacy activities. Furthermore, when caregivers do show up, many programs are story times for the babies that don’t actually teach the caregivers how to engage in early literacy activities at home. Many children may be in daycare during library hours. Childcare for children under the age of one can vary greatly, whether the child is in a daycare center, home daycare, or taken care of by a relative. Some daycares may be aware of each literacy practices, but this will not be the case for all situations. Furthermore, early literacy practices are most effective when done in the home as well as at daycare (Lawhon). 

The effectiveness of early literacy programs are well documented, at least as far as increasing parental knowledge and confidence in early literacy activities. This study seeks to evaluate ways to overcome barriers for educating caregivers on early literacy. Furthermore, most early literacy programs at libraries are evaluated by surveys about caregiver perceptions of the program. This study seeks to evaluate the children's early literacy skills at the end of the program. This leaves this study with two research problems, one that can be measured in the short term and one that is long term. The first question is how can libraries reach more caregivers, especially those who work during the day? One study found that “parents who owned a public library card had greater odds of reading aloud daily to their 6- to 18-month-old child and higher. Parents who visited a public library once a month or more often had greater odds of reading aloud daily” (Chen).. Getting caregivers involved in the library could be imperative for early literacy. The second question is how do these early literacy programs affect the literacy skills in the children involved in the long term? 

This study will evaluate how a program targeted at caregivers will affect early literacy skills on infants. “Individuals who provide modeling are motivators for the young.  Literacy routines such as nursery rhymes, fingerplays, repeat exposure, and story time support early literacy in infants” (Lawhon). Building on other successful studies, this program will create partnerships with local hospitals and daycare providers. Books and information packets will be created by librarians and provided to pediatricians and obstetricians to hand out at well-child checkups. Likewise, these information packets will be provided to daycare providers to handout to parents and to inform their own practices within the daycare. The information packet will include early literacy activities for infants that fall under the sing, talk, read, write, and play categories, alongside information about the library.  

Literature Review 

Many different early literacy programs have been studied across multiple environments. Most show that these early literacy programs increase the confidence, knowledge, and time spent engaged in early literacy activities of the caregiver. Very few have studied the results of the program on the child. This may be due to the difficulty in analyzing a very young child’s early literacy abilities versus asking the caregiver to fill out a survey. Furthermore, many programs are not evaluating how well they reach out to and involve caregivers.  

Bookbabies is a program that gave parents books and reading tips three times over the first two years of the babies lives (Vanobbergen). This program in particular focused on there not being a perfect way to introduce early literacy; any good interaction with a book is a good interaction! This program was found to help parents enjoy early literacy practices with their babies. 

Hush-a-Bye is a program that approaches story time a little differently than most libraries. Rather than the program leader reading a book to the whole group, each parent gets a copy of the book to read along to their baby during the story. Then parents are provided with a different, but related book to read to their baby. Parents reported getting a better idea of what books their child responds to, and admitted choosing books that were aimed at an older age range than their baby. Throughout the session, the program leader also leads them in songs and early literacy tips and activities (Langan). 

“Mother Goose on the Loose: Hatchlings, a program that helps parents nurture their babies through playful literacy practices, both before and immediately after birth” (Sanders, pg 28). This program focuses on expectant parents and follows up with parents of newborns. Rather than ongoing story time, this consists of two separate programs. One single session for expectant parents and four sessions for parents of newborns. The programs teach parents to support early literacy and “focuses on the whole child, building upon a foundation of ritual, repetition, music, movement, learning-by-doing, joy, fostering a non-judgmental atmosphere, and play” (Sanders pg 28). The program even integrates health and child development information such as the importance of tummy time, and visual development. The program can be run in the library, or in the community. The program was evaluated via surveys and all parents in the program responded that the program increased their confidence in their ability to support their baby's early literacy, that they used what they learned in the program, and that the activities helped them bond with their baby. All parents also said they intended to use library resources again in the future. 

Early literacy programs have also had effective programs and partnerships within hospitals. In one study, parents of babies in the NICU engaged in a one hour program on early language and literacy practices. The program was found to increase parent knowledge of early literacy and the majority of parents reported engaging in the activities they learned (Shanty). Better Beginnings is a program that supports parents' knowledge of early literacy practices, and introduces them to library services. This program includes a partnership with local health professionals who provide “reading packs” created by librarians at the 6-8 week health checkup for infants. These packs include board books, nursery rhymes, information about the library, and a DVD about early literacy activities. The program also included library sessions and environments designed to support early literacy. Participants were surveyed over the course of four years, and participants and health staff were interviewed to evaluate the program. “Just before they received the reading pack and became involved in the program, 14 per cent of mothers reported in the pre-program survey that they had already shared books with their baby. One year later, 85 per cent reported sharing books with their baby and, when asked if their levels of confidence in reading to their baby had changed, almost two-thirds (62 per cent) reported an increase in their confidence over the previous year” (Barratt-Pugh).  Parents also reported more involvement in the library. Participants in another study were given children's books at pediatric visits over the first 6 months of the infant's lives. The program was found to increase time spent reading, attitudes towards reading, and the amount of books in the home in comparison to a control group.  “At the 6-month visit relative to the control group, parents in the intervention group reported significantly higher shared reading frequency with 23.8% of the intervention group reading 15 min/d versus 14% of the control group” (Crosh).  However, with 23.8% of the group spending 15 minutes a day reading to their child, it may be possible that more than just access to books may be needed to increase early literacy. 

A few studies have specifically looked at how to reach more caregivers. After struggling with low attendance for parental education programs, this library launched a podcast. Based on downloads of the podcasts they found a 600% increase in engagement over in person sessions (Bouchelle). Another study looked into partnerships in the communities such as with daycares alongside hospitals. Its “findings indicate that (1) partnerships with trusted community organizations enhance parental engagement, (2) logistical barriers such as work schedules and transportation limit access, and (3) parents often value literacy but struggle to incorporate it into daily routines” (Zhang). Challenges found included: program times overlapping with work, having children from multiple age ranges, and fear of child disturbing other patrons. Parent concerns included their children not staying still during story time and fines or damaging books. One parent wished for “grab bags” organized by age. Another article, while not formally evaluated for efficacy, discusses other ways of reaching out to caregivers. This article discusses some programs libraries can run other than story time to support parents. These programs included parent support groups in cooperation with care organizations such as hospitals, pregnancy and new parent classes, parenting classes after the newborn stage, expanded story times that had sections encouraging caregivers to build community with each other, and services for families such as connecting them with other resources in the community. One article explored ways to support library programs aimed at babies including partnerships with local birth units and other service groups, and hosting programs within the library that target parents such as breastfeeding groups. It also calls for more advocacy for early literacy programs (Knoll). One article even focused on reaching male caregivers, who are very underrepresented in early literacy programs. Man in the Moon was developed with the idea that men would feel more comfortable and learn better around other men and being taught by a man. The creator also said that it was best to keep programs like this for men at four or less sessions and to no require pre-registration. The program helps men learn to be silly and sing nursery rhymes with their infants (James). 

One program focused on play, an important but less well-known aspect of early literacy. “Every Child Ready to Read features play as one of the five key early literacy practices”(Ralli, pg 52). This program sets up “play stations" with tips for parents on how to engage in play with their child. This program was found to be successful. The survey results show that “74 percent of respondents reported learning new ways to engage with their children, and 44 percent said they use Read, Play, Grow! activities at home.” (Ralli, pg 52) Play supports literacy, so libraries should support play. Babies engage in exploratory play, which is play that engages the senses (Shortridge). Singing is an important part of early literacy, and one that may even be effective before a child is born. Multiple studies have found that found that pregnant mothers who sang to their unborn children reported stronger bonds with their babies after birth, less crying, less colic, less night wake ups, and lower maternal stress (Persico). 

Research Questions and Hypotheses 

The aim of this research is to evaluate an early literacy program for the effectiveness of its outreach and programming. As such, the research will answer the following questions: 

Question 1: Will involving community partners in an early literacy program increase 	caregiver participation compared to the current program? 

Question 2: Will increasing caregiver knowledge of early literacy skills affect their child's 	early literacy skills compared to children not involved in the program? 

From these two questions the following null hypotheses were derived: 

Hypothesis 1: Community partnerships will increase caregiver participation in early 	literacy programs. 

Hypothesis 2:  Caregiver knowledge of early literacy skills will increase their child's early 	literacy skills. 

In the event that the null hypotheses are rejected, the following alternative hypotheses 

will be considered: 

Hypothesis 3: Community partnerships will not increase caregiver participation in early 	literacy programs. 

Hypothesis 4: Caregiver knowledge of early literacy skills will not increase their child's 	early literacy skills. 

Methodology 

 

This study will measure for two factors. The first is caregiver participation. The library keeps track of participation for its current early literacy program. This program is a story time for babies once a week at the library. The library will continue to track participation in story time to see if the early literacy outreach program affects it.  

Data Collection: Early Literacy Skills 

Data collection can be costly and time intensive, especially for measuring something like early literacy skills. To measure the effectiveness of this program caregivers will be asked to fill out a survey about what early literacy skills they used and how often. When the children in the program enter kindergarten, the caregivers will be asked to submit the results of the reading readiness screener that is required in Wisconsin by Act 20. These results will be compared to the general population. This will be an ongoing process in order to get a few years of results. 

Data Analysis and Hypothesis Testing 

Once the data is collected, it will be entered into a spread sheet. The mode, mean median, range, interquatrile range, and standard deviation will be calculated for the data. The z-scores will be calculated to determine if the sample mean is reflective of the population mean. Finally, a two-tail t test will be used to test the null hypothesis using a p-value of 0.05 for the significance level.  

Significance and Limitations 

While many studies have analyzed the effects of early literacy programs on caregiver confidence and knowledge, few have actually looked at the long-term effects on the children themselves. Furthermore, many outreach programs are not reaching many caregivers, so ways to reach them such as through community partners need to be tested. A program that can increase early literacy in children will ultimately not be effective if it’s not reaching the children. 	In order to save resources on data this study uses data from the general population rather than a formal control group. It is also likely that caregivers may drop out of this study or not respond by the time their child is in kindergarten and taking the test the study is using to determine long term effectiveness. This study will also rely on participants signing up to submit results after receiving the information packet from a community partner.  

Conclusion 

Early literacy activities are vital for infants, but a mystery to many caregivers. Early literacy programs can be so important for reaching out to and educating caregivers. However, caregivers can be a difficult group to reach as they often work or are otherwise busy during library hours. Outreach programs are necessary to reach this group and could encourage the use of library resources for early literacy. Early literacy programs also need to be evaluated for long term effectiveness. While we know caregivers feel good about the effects of early literacy programs, we lack evidence on how these programs affect the children involved long term. This research proposal would fill in these gaps in early literacy research.

Public Library Quarterly (New York, N.Y.), 1–15.		https://doi.org/10.1080/01616846.2025.2497574  Following backwards design, I started with what I wanted my students to learn. I knew I wanted my lesson to be for high school students in a school library setting. I also knew I wanted to focus my lesson on artificial intelligence, and that I wanted students to know how and when to use it. The first part of backwards design is to “determine the intended results of the session by writing learning outcomes” (Saunders, 2020). Since my goal was for students to understand how and when to use AI, my learning outcomes were “students will evaluate strengths and weaknesses of ChatGPT” and “students will determine appropriate use of generative AI according to school policy”. These goals are meant to be specific, so although I started with a learning goal that sounded something like “understand generative artificial intelligence” this was too vague. I narrowed it down and used words like “evaluate” and “determine” to make what I wanted them to learn both more specific and measurable. Even then, I started with just “students will determine appropriate use of generative AI”. After receiving feedback, I realized that appropriate use is very dependent on the setting, and I added “according to school policy” so the lesson would just focus on using it as a tool for schoolwork. These learning outcomes don’t reach the top of the pyramid of Blooms Taxonomy of Learning since the students don’t create anything (Saunders, 2020). However, I think these learning goals are an appropriate step before students would be ready to truly use generative AI in the process of creating something unique. I believe this lesson most closely fit in “analyze” for when students “determine” use of generative AI, but could also fit under “evaluate” for when students “evaluate” generative AI. Based on the age of the students and the content being taught, I didn’t think a lesson that used “remember” or “understand” was necessary to build up to higher order skills.  

The second part of backwards design is to “identify assessments, or activities, experiments, performances, or tasks in which students could engage to demonstrate their learning” (Saunders, 2020). At this point I needed a way to show if they learned to evaluate the strength and weaknesses of generative AI and determine appropriate use of it. I knew I preferred direct assessments like worksheets because I was looking for quantifiable proof of what they learned. I was less interested in indirect assessments because “while students tell us that they have learned something through indirect assessment, they are not showing us what they have learned, and we cannot be certain that students are accurate in their reflections or self-perceptions” (Saunders, 2020). I didn’t think an indirect assessment would have any strength in this scenario since the lesson focuses on what I would consider to be basic and foundational skills of AI. If I ran into a situation where I thought students were anxious or stressed about this topic or assignment, or if this were one part of a longer running class, I would use indirect assessments to gauge student needs so I could work on modifying the lesson.  

I chose to use a formative assessment, think-pair-share, to get an idea of students understanding, and so the students can learn from each other. This assessment ended up being later in the lesson, but I thought that applying the information they gathered over the course of the lesson to evaluate AI would be the portion they would be most likely to struggle with. This is the part I wanted to check in on, make sure they are on the right track, and be able to correct any misunderstandings. I also like this method because students who are struggling but not asking for help may be able to find more understanding through their classmates sharing their ideas.  

Some of the actual worksheet I used for the summative assessment is done throughout the lesson. I started with the last four questions in mind for the summative assessment, but later realized it made the most sense for the steps leading up to them to be included. The first and second part are meant to help guide them through the lesson and have them gather information into one place to refer back to for the questions at the end. They also gather this information directly into the worksheet so the instructor can refer back to it when grading part 3 of the worksheet. How well students perform on each part of the lesson can also help the instructor identify if there is a misunderstanding and a part of the lesson needs to be reworked in some way in the future.  

I also wanted to try to keep both assessments authentic. I wanted to see the evidence of their thought process as they go through filling out the worksheet. I didn’t want to tell them the strengths and weaknesses of generative AI then have them list them back on a test or worksheet. I also acknowledge the strengths and weaknesses of AI depend on the topic and desired outcome. Some students might find that using generative AI had a lot of strengths for their topic, while others might have a topic that AI struggles with. I also liked the think-pair-share assessment because it gives students the opportunity to hear about these unique experiences that other students might have had with the generative AI. I wanted them to discover the strengths and weaknesses as they explored generative AI, which is a skill that they can carry on going forward.  

I included a rubric for the worksheet since correct answers aren’t necessarily obvious, even to the instructor. There weren’t any specific strengths or weaknesses that I was looking for them to identify, I just wanted to see if they put thought and reasoning into what they considered a strength or weakness. Since we discuss the school rules for using generative AI, I do want to see that they consider these rules when identifying situations to use or not use AI. I attempted to make the criteria for the rubric specific without needlessly quantifying it. Ultimately the rubric came down to whether or not they filled out each question and if they provided enough reasoning. I debated whether to include answers being “2-3” sentences because this could be needlessly quantified. However, I thought “showed evidence of critical reasoning” was too vague, and ultimately 2-3 sentences was a good goal for them to both state their answer and brief reasoning behind it. I debated whether to grade the first two parts of the worksheet, since these parts don’t technically show if they learned what they were supposed to. However, I decided these two parts are vital to the student developing skills, and I was concerned that students would put less effort into them if they knew they weren’t graded. If they didn’t take part 1 and 2 seriously, they might struggle more with part 3. There were some things I chose not to grade, that I might have included if I knew this lesson was part of a larger sequence of lessons. The lesson assumes that students have basic computer skills, and that they specifically have the research skills to find reliable sources. If this were part of an ongoing class where they had learned to find sources, I might have included this on the rubric. As is, finding sources was not part of the lesson so I did not choose to grade based on the sources they used.  

Once I knew that my learning goals were “students will evaluate strengths and weaknesses of ChatGPT” and “students will determine appropriate use of generative AI according to school policy”, that I would use think-pair-share as a formative assessment so students could discuss and share their thoughts, and that I would use questions asking “What are the strengths of ChatGPT”, “What are the weaknesses of ChatGPT”, “When could you use ChatGPT for school?” and “When should you not use ChatGPT for school?” I needed to plan how the lesson would be delivered. I’ll admit that I already had thoughts on this part when starting the design, but I did my best to not let this influence the learning outcomes and assessments. I think I did an okay job of this because the idea I had in mind ended up needing to be modified based on the learning outcomes and assessments. The third part of backwards design is to “plan the sequence of material and activities and think about the steps they will take to capture learners’ interest and keep them engaged throughout the lesson” (Saunders, 2020).  

To maximize active learning, I tried to keep any lectures short. The instructor might spend around ten minutes introducing generative AI and the assignment, and another couple of minutes discussing school policy on generative AI. These short lectures were the most effective way to quickly deliver the necessary information that students need to complete the assessments. The lecture on using generative AI is also demonstrative, which can “increase learner engagement with lectures” (Saunders, 2020). The first lesson, and overall lesson, also has a hook to get students interest. “Are you smarter than AI?” is a fun challenge to get students to engage with the assignment. The overall structure of the lesson does not fully follow problem-based learning but does take inspiration from it. The lesson does start with a question for students to explore, “are you smarter than AI?”. However for the lesson to fully follow problem-based learning the question would need to have more possible answers, and the students would need to be given more freedom to choose how they research. The parts of problem-based learning that this lesson takes inspiration from, is asking a question that relates to the real world for the students, and allowing them to find the answers for themselves instead of telling them or showing them where to find an answer. Think-pair-share is great for encouraging students to speak up in discussion. Because they talk to one other person first, they can gain confidence to share in front of the whole group. Even if they aren’t up to speaking up that day, they will still have discussed their ideas with at least one other person. The worksheet also takes inspiration from graphic organizers. While it’s not aimed at getting information out of a lecture, it helps students focus on the information they need to find to complete their task.  

The lesson does not fully align with any one learning theory, but most closely aligns with humanism and cognitivism. I did not design the lesson with a particular learning theory in mind, but I’m not surprised to discover these two theories align with the lesson since I knew my teaching style tends to lean towards them. I know my teaching style tends to lean towards personal model because I overall like to guide students through activities. I have a lot of interest in acting more as a facilitator and using more problem-based learning, but I’ve never been in a situation where I felt I had enough time to fully embrace this. The lesson aligns with humanism because it uses student interest as a motivating factor. My chloe is that since students are choosing something that they have prior knowledge of, they’ll want to prove they know more than the AI, and they’ll be more interested in participating because they get to focus on something they like. I was also very excited to realize that ChatGPT can be used in multiple languages. Students would be able to use their preferred language when using ChatGPT, which aligns with humanism. The lesson also aligns with cognitivism because students are using prior knowledge to develop understanding of a new topic. I did not intend this, but while looking back over readings on learning theory I realized that this lesson follows Gagné’s nine conditions for learning very closely, if out of order (Saunders, 2020). The lesson starts with a stimulating question to get attention, the instructor identifies what they’re learning, students use prior knowledge, new knowledge is presented and demonstrated, students are given time to practice, and an activity is used to access performance.

Introduction  

 Case #2.14 states that the new director of the Kenoba Public Library created a new policy "prohibit[ing] sleeping in the library and occupying the same table or desk for longer than two hours" (Buchanan, E.A. et al., 2009). The new director created this policy due to the two-mile range of distance between the public library and the homeless shelter (Buchanan E.A. et al., 2009). The shelter has an enforcement that "between the hours of 10:00 A.M. and 3:00 P.M.'' residents must be gone from the premise which resulted in them going to the public library (Buchanan E.A. et al., 2009). The director of the Kenoba Public Library stated that he does not want the "real patrons" "scared off by the smell or sight of those people”  (Buchanan E.A. et al., 2009). This statement provokes the question of the ethical obligation the public library has to its homeless population. Furthermore, it calls into question the laws in place regarding the homeless population in public spaces and what is being done to assist them.  

The actions of the Kenoba Public Library are analyzed in four sections throughout the paper. The first is focused on the director's new policy and how the wording used within it is affecting the homeless population.  The second section is on the question of the rights of the homeless population within the public library setting. The third section covers the ethical and legal questions regarding the standards in place for the homeless within the public library. Finally, the last section will focus on the policies the American Library Association (ALA) has in place for people that are in the situation of homelessness.  

Kenoba Public Library Director’s New Policy  

           The policy outlined in the introduction doesn’t directly ban people experiencing homelessness; there is no direct language to ban those specific individuals. However, the policy is designed to exclude them. This is supported by the statement given along with the policy. This is not an uncommon set of rules. Looking at the conduct policy for Milwaukee Public Libraries, numerous rules can be seen as determinants for people experiencing homelessness. Most notably in the section for behavior that is not allowed: sleeping, creating an offensive atmosphere from poor hygiene, using restrooms for loitering or bathing, and carrying excessive items defined by the item's ability to fit under a chair (Code of Conduct, n.d.). All of these rules, while not directly banning the homeless population, are designed in their intent and wording to prevent them. In a legal sense, intent matters but is arguable. If somebody wanted to argue the Kenoba policy they could use that extra statement to prove a prejudice against people experiencing homelessness, but it could also be argued it isn’t included in the official policy (Stucke, 2012). More so than the intent, the wording itself is very important when it comes to policy. Take the case of Armstrong vs. District of Columbia Public Library: where Armstrong, a man currently experiencing homelessness, was barred from a library for violating their “objectionable appearance” rule. He argued that the rule and his rejection from the library were violations of his First and Fifth Amendment rights. The case was won because of the wording of the rule. It was found to be too vague, making the ruling of what is “objectionable” up to the staff and could be different from day to day and person to person. There is no articulable standard and therefore no process to amend if you are found to be violating the rule (Armstrong vs. District of Columbia Public Library, 2001). The Kenoba library policy could easily have a similar issue with what is defined as “legitimate” business that warrants a table for more than two hours. That is a determination that is left up to staff and could change from day to day and person to person.  

           People experiencing homelessness are often still employed. According to the National Alliance to End Homelessness over 50% of people residing in shelters were employed full or part-time in the year they lived in the shelter. These people are often also educated and could have plenty of reasons to use computers or materials available in the library. Their First Amendment right protects their access to this information. People who are facing housing disparities may not have consistent access to the internet, which can keep them at a digital divide and disadvantage. Libraries are often the bridge for people in the digital divide (Jaeger et al., 2012). There is an ethical responsibility for librarians to provide access to a diverse population, regardless of personal prejudice, like those expressed by the director in the personal statement (ALA, 2017).  

What rights do homeless individuals have in public libraries? 

  

 Do homeless patrons have the same rights as anyone else that steps into the public library? Does everyone who enters Kenoba Public Library have equal footing? A federal judge declared that an individual cannot be banned from a library because they are homeless (Hanley, 1991). Public libraries protect an individual’s First Amendment “right to receive information and ideas” (ALA, 2008). 

        	However, a public library is a “limited public forum” that is allowed to create policies and enforce them (Caldwell-Stone, 2019). What exactly does that mean in legal terms? It means that the “government agency administering the space is only obligated to allow those First Amendment activities that are consistent with the nature of the forum, even if the facility is open to the public” (Caldwell-Stone, 2019). Kenoba Public Library can argue that a no-sleeping policy is within their power to enforce, as sleeping in a library is not consistent with a library’s mission of serving patrons. However, this policy would have to apply to all patrons, for instance, students falling asleep on textbooks. 

The same can be said for the two-hour rule, it would have to be regulated equally and posted in a way so all patrons knew about the rule ahead of time to gain permission. The staff also could not discriminate towards people experiencing homelessness for “smell” as mentioned by the Kenoba director unless an actual rule was created. However, if a library policy uses “smell to mitigate a health hazard” then the “library focuses on providing access and a safe environment for patrons and employees—while avoiding judgments rooted in subjectivity” (WNYLRC, 2020). 

Making sure that constitutional rights are not being violated within their limited public forum parameters is important and has proven to sometimes be tricky as it pertains to homeless individuals. “In the U.S. Constitution, the phrase "due process" appears twice: in the Fifth Amendment and in the Fourteenth Amendment. Both Amendments guarantee due process when someone is denied "life, liberty, or property” (Legal Information Institute, n.d.). “A well-defined appeals process must be available to patrons who challenge policies” (Dowd, 2018) at all public libraries.  

        	Eighth Amendment rights have been challenged as it relates to homeless encampments that libraries try to deter from forming on the exterior library property. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has set precedent for its jurisdiction that no unsheltered persons can be criminalized for camping if no other alternative place is available (Zulkey, 2019). And the court cited that forcing the homeless to move their campouts (if no alternative was available) would violate the Eighth Amendment’s protection against “cruel and unusual punishment” (Zulkey, 2019). 

The Kenoba Public Library must ask if they are opening themselves to lawsuits over the matter of the First, Fifth & Fourteenth, and perhaps the Eighth Amendment rights granted to all individuals that enter their library and who might remain on the outdoor premises.  

In addition to constitutional rights, the principles of the American Library Association’s Library Bill of Rights must be considered. “Questions do arise concerning application of these principles to specific library practices” (ALA, 2006). Article V declares: “A person’s right to use a library should not be denied or abridged because of origin, age, background, or views” (ALA, 2006). This could apply to the two hour time limit being set in response to homeless individuals. 

        	Enforcement of these policies varies between libraries, making the rights of homeless patrons a gray area. This can create a legal and ethical debate, as well as one of compassion. Will the Kenoba director give options and resources to the homeless? Or just ask them to leave?  

What ethical and legal principles are significant here? 

When creating a policy within a library there are both ethical and legal principles to be considered. An ethical principle is a guideline or rule created based on what is regarded as appropriate or correct. In 1939, the American Library Association enacted a Code of Ethics. Principle 9 of the code states, “We affirm the inherent dignity and rights of every person. We work to recognize and dismantle systemic and individual biases; to confront inequity and oppression; to enhance diversity and inclusion; and to advance racial and social justice in our libraries, communities, profession, and associations through awareness, advocacy, education, collaboration, services, and allocation of resources and spaces” (ALA, 2017).   

The responsibility of upholding these principles lies within libraries and communities, in this case the Kenoba Public Library. In New Zealand, a study was conducted to investigate homeless men’s interactions in the library to better understand public perceptions (Hodgetts, 2008). The results of this study support incorporating ethical principles, such as creating a space for mutual respect. One homeless patron named Tom describes spending his daytime hours in the library as part of his daily routine and opportunity to participate in the community, “we’re just reading books and doing what everybody else uses the library for to read and have time out” (Hodgetts, 2008). This idea of participating in society like ‘everybody else’ is summarized by Don Mitchell in 2003 “By claiming space in public, by creating public spaces, social groups themselves become public. Only in public space, for example, can homeless people represent themselves as a legitimate part of ‘the public'” (Hodgetts, 2008). In this version of a public space, it is possible to support the ethical principles of inclusion by overcoming bias through confronting inequity.  

Legal principles are government regulations, which impact government entities such as a public library. Within the United States there are policies that either criminalize or protect citizens experiencing homelessness. Those that criminalize place restrictions on the homeless in public spaces. While libraries are accessible to the public, they can enact individual policies. The director’s new policy is based on two factors: not sleeping in the library and not occupying a table for more than two hours without permission. In a report conducted by the National Law Center on Homelessness and Poverty, 53% of cities have laws against sitting in public, or loitering, and 18% have bans on sleeping in public, with 27% specifying specific public spaces where sleeping is banned (National Law Center on Homlessness and Poverty, 2015).   

Alternatively, to combat potential discrimination there are legal protections for people experiencing homelessness. As previously stated the 1st, 5th, 14th, and potentially 8th Amendments provide federal protections. On a smaller scale, three states, Illinois, Rhode Island and Connecticut each have a Homeless Bill of Rights, protections against discrimination based on housing status (Sheffield, 2015). The director of Kenoba Public Library was quoted as saying “This library is not a shelter, and if they aren’t paying taxes, they have no right to be here” (Buchanan & Henderson, 2009). This statement suggests that patrons without permanent housing shouldn’t be allowed in the library. Under a Homeless Bill of Right protection, homeless residents are required to ‘receive equal treatment by government agencies,’ meaning Kenoba would be in direct violation (Sheffield, 2015). 

On a larger scale, the United Nations recognizes that adequate housing is a human right, and a responsibility of both the private and public sectors. As quoted from the Universal Declaration on Human Rights “the human right to adequate housing is the right of every woman, man, youth and child to gain and sustain a safe and secure home and community in which to live in peace and dignity” (Sheffield, 2015). As a public entity of the community and an information hub, according to the U.N., it would be the shared responsibility of the library to provide resources that would assist the homeless in finding secure housing rather than excluding them completely.  

American Library Association’s policy on services to the poor and homeless. 

            The American Library Association (ALA), a nationally trusted organization that provides leadership for libraries, would not agree with this director’s reasoning for their policy. However, they have guidelines that support parts of the policy. This director wanted to discourage homeless people from using the library by banning sleeping in the library, and limiting table use to two hours unless patrons had “legitimate business.” This director reasoned that since homeless people don’t pay taxes, they shouldn’t receive library services. 

The ALA does not have any policy specifically referencing sleeping in the library; however, they say this director cannot use this rule to specifically target homeless people. Policies and regulations that impose restrictions on library access should “be enforced consistently and not in a manner intended to benefit or disfavor any person or group in an arbitrary or capricious manner” (ALA, 2007). This library can enforce its no sleeping rule, but it would need to enforce it for everyone, not just people who appear homeless. 

Once again, the ALA does not specifically reference time limits on table use, but they say all policies should “avoid arbitrary distinctions between individuals or classes of users and denying or abridging a person’s right to use library resources, services, or facilities based upon arbitrary distinctions such as origin, age, background, or views” (ALA, 2007). A two-hour limit on library tables would abridge a person’s right to library resources and facilities, and additionally targeting people who appear homeless would once again go against ALA policies. 

The ALA directly addresses how libraries should treat homeless populations, “Access to library and information resources, services, and technologies is essential for all people, especially the economically disadvantaged, who may experience isolation, discrimination and prejudice or barriers to education, employment, and housing” (American Library Association, 2012). Some ways the ALA recommends supporting homeless populations within the library include eliminating overdue fines, purchasing materials that address homelessness and poverty, training staff on services for people in poverty, and even partnering with other organizations that support homeless populations, such as shelters. (ALA, 2012).  

Conclusion 

The ALA states that everybody should have the ability to access "library and information resources, services, and technologies" due to it being "essential for all people" (ALA, 2012). And it is also stated that libraries are "government[ agencies]" and therefore "only obligated to allow those First Amendment activities that are consistent with the nature of the forum, even if the facility is open to the public”(Caldwell-Stone, 2019). In the realm of public space, there are rules and policies that all members of the public are expected to follow. There is a gray area for some of the wording within these policies where bias can take form. A gray area in which bias has taken root is in the new director of the Kenoba Public Library. Their new policy "prohibit[s] sleeping in the library and occupying the same table or desk for longer than two hours" and that wording is biased with the intention to ban the homeless population from that space. (Buchanan, E.A. et al., 2009). The public library is a public space for all, and that includes the homeless population. Therefore, future policymakers should keep that in mind when evaluating the intent of their library rules and regulations.

Score is 15/15  This class filled in some gaps in my knowledge of children’s literature and has made me feel much more confident in working with kid's books. I have found myself approaching aspects of the library in very different ways than I did before.  The three areas that I feel this class had the biggest impact on my understanding of are artwork in children’s books, what children want to read, and the importance of nonfiction and early readers/chapter books.  

Previous to this class, I undervalued artwork in children’s books. I thought good art could be a nice bonus but didn’t consider it necessary. I had a larger focus on the text, which is likely because I usually either skimmed books for content or was focused on reading them aloud. I’ve learned how important art can be to children’s books whether it’s on the cover, the title page, or the pages. However, after starting this class I’ve been paying attention to how my students choose books and realized they start with the cover. If the cover has low quality art or isn’t interesting looking, they’re not even going to pick it up. I’ve always heard not to judge a book by its cover, but I will from now on because I know my students will. I also learned that a good picture book has art that helps tell the story, and sometimes this art starts well before the words do. The words and the art work together to tell the story, and if either were missing the story would not be the same. This has caused me to slow down while reading picture books or graphic novels and pay more attention to the art so I can point out the story telling elements to my students.  

I have a better grasp of what my students want when they’re looking for books, although I think this is complicated and can be very different for everyone. Ultimately, many students want a book that they can relate to. This can be as simple as a hobby, or as complex as something that will reflect their life experiences. Students wanting books they can relate to is one of the reasons why it’s important to have a diverse collection that represents all people. Students want books with characters that look like them, live like them, and have families like theirs. They should be able to find these authentic, high quality books that represent them in the library. This is something that I always realized was important but didn’t know how to measure or know if my collection was diverse enough. A diversity audit sounds like such a monumental task for one person and 16,000 books, but I realize the importance of it and have been puzzling out how I can make one work. 

Finally, I learned that nonfiction and early readers/chapter books are a lot more interesting than I thought. I used to place more value on picture books, chapter books, and graphic novels. I thought that nonfiction was necessary but boring, and early readers/chapter books were just for transitioning from picture books to chapter books. I have since learned that both of these types of books have enough merit to stand on their own. I previously just thought of traditional texts when it came to nonfiction, but I discovered a love of narrative and active nonfiction in this class. I also thought early readers/chapter books were too boring and simple. After learning what goes into creating a book that is simple enough for young children to read on their own, but complex enough to keep their attention, I am so much more impressed with a good early reader/chapter book. I also have realized how important early chapter books are for maintaining students' love of reading. I realized that my disinterest in these books have affected my library. Because I didn’t find them interesting, they haven’t gotten as much of my attention. I think this has influenced how my students feel about these books, so I’m working on revamping my nonfiction section and creating an early chapter book section. I ran a report for books in my nonfiction section that have not been checked out more than a handful of times in the last fifteen years and were published more than ten years ago and I have nearly 3000 nonfiction books that fit these parameters that I have been going through and weeding. This is just my starting point, but I’m hoping that once I’ve weeded out the dated books, added new, exciting nonfiction books of various types, and added new signage, that I can drive up excitement and circulation in this section.  

This class has had a profound impact on how I approach books in my library. I have developed an appreciation for how art is used to tell the story in children's literature. I believe I have a better understanding of what my students want to read and how I can move forward with making sure my collection has books that they can relate to. I’m more excited about nonfiction and early readers/chapter books, which I think will increase my student’s interest in these books.  I’m really looking forward to all of these projects that I have been inspired to do or try, and how they will affect the way my students read. 
 
A Teen Advisory Board (TAB) can be so many things but will ultimately be shaped by the teens themselves. My goal in creating a TAB would be to involve teens in the library and greater community, build their skills, and (this is hardest to measure) ultimately give them a meaningful experience. The first part of the goal would be measurable by comparing numbers for teen participation in library events and use of the library before TAB is started to these numbers after TAB is started. If more teens are engaging with the library whether through library events, using library services, or just within TAB then TAB has met its first goal. The second part of the goal would be harder to measure, but could be done through surveys on teens' skills relating to an event before and after that event, or as they join and leave TAB. Teens need to support their community, and feel supported by their community so I believe TAB will inherently be a meaningful experience for them (Developmental Assets Framework).  

I purposely left my goal for TAB a little vague because I believe the teens involved in TAB should have a voice in determining the purpose of the group. I want to “recognize teens as thinking human beings who have ideas, interests, and passions that are valid and important” (Braun, 2018). I have set some structure in saying that TAB should be involved in the community and build their skills because teens still need some structure, or they might take too much on or lose sight of what the group is for. However, I think there needs to be a lot of room for adaptability for teens to have a say in how TAB is involved with the community and what skills they build. The Young Adult Library Services Association says we need to work on “embracing our role as facilitator rather than expert” when working with teens (Braun, 2018). I’m not an expert on teens, so I structured my goal to facilitate the teens of the group to create their own mission statement as part of the creation of TAB. I think it would make sense to review and amend the mission statement of TAB each year with the teens currently in the program so they can have a full understanding and voice, and so it can adapt to the needs of the teens currently in the community.  

According to librarians who have started and advised TABs, recruiting and retaining teens is the most difficult part. To recruit teens, I would start with events for teens already being put on by the library. If the library I was starting a TAB for didn’t already have decent outreach into the teen community, I would want to start with that. Ironically, a TAB would improve outreach to the teen community, but I think attempting to start a TAB before you have some rapport with the teen community could cause the group to fall apart before it begins due to lack of interest or engagement. Developing these connections with teens before starting the program will help them feel more connected to and comfortable with the library, and it's important for teens to have meaningful relationships with adults outside of their family (Developmental Assets Framework). I would also make sure we have a relationship with local schools and that we have events and outreach at the schools. I would start recruitment with teens who already are involved with the library and have come to multiple events. I would ask them if they would be interested in joining and how they would recruit more teens. I would start by focusing on teens in grades 9-12 because they’re able to handle more responsibility and are more likely to have their own transportation, but I would like to include younger teens after the program has been developed possibly as junior member or as their own group. Besides working on developing rapport with local teens at library events (in the library, community, and at school) I would want to develop a social media presence for the library that focuses on teens. “More than 81% of online teens use some kind of social media” so I think it's a good place to market and get teens attention (Braun, 2018). Eventually, I would ask TAB to help me with social media because they will be more up to date on what gets teen’s attention than I am. 

Next, I would create a TAB application to hand out at events to teens who are interested. The application would list what TAB is, what they get out of it, and what would be expected of them. It would have them fill out some basic information about themselves and their contact information, and have questions about why they want to join TAB, what their hobbies and interests are, and what skills they think they have that would be useful for TAB. I don’t think I would necessarily turn down any applicants, but I think applying will help them understand what they are signing up for and take it seriously. Besides recruiting at library events for teens I don’t think I would want to spend too long on initial recruitment before the first meeting because excitement might lessen if it’s too drawn out. After I’ve found at least a small group of teens who are interested, I would survey them to find out a time and location that will work for them. Teens have busy schedules so I wouldn’t want to choose a time just based on what works for me because it might not work for them and I would be left with few or no teens coming to the TAB. For example, if the majority of teens who are interested are all at the same high school and want to meet right after school, it might make the most sense to have meetings at the high school. 

It’s important to “seek out and listen to the voices of adolescents who are often marginalized and may not currently be seen as library users” so I want to make sure this is something I take into consideration (Braun, 2018). There are five high schools in the county that the library serves. Two are near the main library and have 1490 and 178 students. One challenge could be in how to reach teens at the smaller, rural schools. Two have library branches in town, but the high schools for these areas have 174 and 124 students. The last high school is 20 minutes away from any library in the county and has 338 students. I believe it would make sense to have one TAB for the county. If we attempted to have one for each area, we may not have a staff member available to be the advisor at the smaller locations, and they may not be able to recruit enough students from the smaller high schools. The challenge would be in how to involve students from these high schools. One possibility would be having an option for virtual meetings, or for rural teens to attend the meetings virtually. Another option would be to find a way to offer transportation. I would also want to look into how to reach groups of teens that aren’t at these high schools, like students who are homeschooled.  

For expectations, I would ask teens to commit to a year when joining TAB and understand that our main goal is to create experiences for other teens in the library and community. I would start with once-a-month whole group meetings, with the possibility of smaller group meetings for teens who have committed to working on a specific project. However, I’m keeping in mind that this could change. I would want teens in the initial group to help develop expectations like how many meetings you can miss without permission and still be in TAB. As mentioned, I mainly view myself as the facilitator for this, so I would want to go into this with the groundwork for things that need to be done, but overall help guide the teens in developing TAB and the programs it does. Besides developing these expectations for what responsibilities members of TAB have, I would also want them to set some ground rules for interacting with each other. Teens need positive interactions with their peers (Developmental Assets Framework) and they need to work together for TAB to work, so I would ask them to set expectations for things like “don’t yuck my yum” and how they will handle disagreements.  

At the group's first meeting when we’re determining what TAB will be, I would also survey the teens about what they’re interested in doing for their library and community. With these ideas in mind, I would start each meeting with a framework for ideas. I would probably have a topic/theme in mind for each meeting and start the meeting with an icebreaker question or activity about that topic. The topic could be based on what the teens said they’re interested in or something the library needs, but either way it would be a broad topic, so the teens have room to make it into what they are interested in. I might give some background information on the topic, then ask the teens to start brainstorming a few ideas for programs they can create for the library.  

For example, March is Youth Art Month, so a few months before March I might use that for the theme of the meeting (especially if they have indicated they are interested in art) and ask them to come up with program ideas based on it. I would not come with my own idea for Youth Art Month, like a comic making activity, and tell them what we need to do and how to do it because that would take their voice away and rob them of the opportunity to create their own program and learn all of the skills that go alongside that. However, I would attempt to guide them without being too obtrusive. Teens have a desire to “connect and create community without being pushed or made powerless by adults” (Campana, 2019). I would hold them responsible for the things they want to do, so they will also need to come up with a plan for their ideas and how they will implement them. My chloe is that this will help them realize if they have an idea that is too ambitious or unlikely to happen. Once they have programs ideas and an initial plan, I would have the group vote on which ones they want to do. I don’t have a set number of programs because if they have a bunch of people who want to help with a program, they could do multiple, but if they only have a few they’ll need to stick to one program. Depending on how many programs they are doing, they would need to create sub-committees to work on each one and have members take on responsibility for the tasks that need to be done. They would be able to individually check in with me about their tasks, rather than having a whole separate meeting for each program, but if they need additional collaboration time, they would be able to have an extra meeting with their sub-committee. I’m hoping that retainment will be possible through offering them a meaningful experience. There are other things I could offer for them to do, like volunteering to shelve at the library, book reviews, or helping choose books for the teen section but I would like to see TAB develop organically so I wouldn’t require these.  

I realize my entire plan is vague, but this is because I want to leave room for adaptability based on the teens in my community. My intention is not to let them do whatever they want, I think the choices I make for TAB always need to come back to its goal- is it getting teens involved in the library, building their skills, and giving them a meaningful experience? However, I admit I don’t understand everything about teens, so I want to leave plenty of room for TAB to become something that they want to be involved in.
